author: Procopius of Gaza
occasion: Procopius playfully praises his correspondent's eloquence and, through the imagined voice of Dionysus, defends a poor man (likely the correspondent or a third party) devoted to the Muses and Graces, arguing that wealth of words and wealth of money cannot coexist.
argument: Procopius opens by telling his addressee that he truly carries the Graces on his tongue, as if a shrine to them were established in him. He then introduces Dionysus, who might be blamed for overlooking a poor man who dreams of tribute/taxes even from his bedding, but who is otherwise devoted to the Muses and Graces. In an imagined speech, Dionysus explains that one cannot be rich in both words and money, and that he withdrew the grape clusters so that he himself might cultivate the man's tongue more, just as cicadas fed on dew contain the Muses within themselves. Procopius concludes that one should be content with present circumstances, since singing alone can make tax collectors immediately forget about money.

outline.move: Procopius praises the addressee's eloquence by saying he carries the Graces on his tongue, and introduces Dionysus as a potential critic of a poor man devoted to the Muses and Graces.

Procopius addresses Dionysus directly, asking why he did not come in abundance and make the vines heavy with fruit, wishing that he had also trodden the wine-presses and danced the bacchic dance so that none of the must was empty; from which, having wealth nobly, the man would have danced for pleasure and been more musical.
Dionysus is imagined to reply that one cannot be rich in both words and money, and that he withdrew the grape clusters so that he himself might cultivate the man's tongue more.

The imagined Dionysus compares the man to cicadas fed on dew who contain the Muses within themselves, and one might say upon hearing them that they were once human beings and have become cicadas; Procopius concludes that one should be content with present circumstances, and if tax collectors trouble one, singing alone can make them immediately forget about money.

cast.name: Dionysus
cast.who: The god of wine, invoked as the one who could have made the poor man rich through the vine.

cast.name: Ariadne
cast.who: Mythical woman whom Dionysus was defeated by and with whom he lived as spouse on Naxos.

cast.name: The Graces
cast.who: Goddesses of charm and eloquence, said to dwell on the addressee's tongue.

voices.speaker: Dionysus (imagined by Procopius)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'Βούλει μαθεῖν καὶ ὅ τι πρὸς ταῦτά φησιν ὁ Διόνυσος;' and then quoted with ὡς, φησὶν, and direct speech

key_terms.sense: The Graces, goddesses of charm and eloquence, here representing the addressee's graceful speech.
The Muses, representing poetic and literary cultivation.
Tribute or taxes, the wealth the poor man dreams of.
New wine, the produce that would have made the man rich.
Cicadas, a traditional image of poets who live on dew and song.
Tax collectors or agents who demand payment.
